title: Aluminum
objective: After this level you can explain why aluminum was once more precious than gold.
summary: Aluminum is the crust's most common metal but never occurs as metal, so it once outvalued gold. In 1886 Hall and Heroult freed it with electricity, and its price collapsed.

cards.headline: An emperor's best guests ate with aluminum cutlery.
cards.body: Napoleon III's most important guests got aluminum; the rest made do with mere silver. Today the same metal turns up in cooking pots and airplanes. What changed?

cards.fact: Aluminum is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, about 8 percent by weight.
cards.context: Only oxygen and silicon are more plentiful, and Level 35's iron comes after it. So why was it ever rare? Because aluminum is chemically active, it never occurs as a metal in nature. It's locked tight in compounds in rocks. Abundant everywhere, and for a long time out of reach.

cards.headline: Once more valuable than gold
cards.body: In the mid-1800s, aluminum was more valuable than gold. Only small amounts could be pried out of its compounds, at great cost. That's why an emperor showed off aluminum cutlery. It was a showpiece metal, and a remarkably light one: aluminum is only about one-third as dense as iron or copper.

cards.headline: 1886: electricity sets it free
cards.body: In 1886, Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Heroult in France independently cracked it: pass electricity through purified alumina, a compound of aluminum and oxygen, dissolved in a molten mineral called cryolite. Hall worked partly in his family's woodshed. By 1891 aluminum cost less than $1 a pound. A treasure fit for an emperor became a metal for cooking pots.

mascot.line: A world-changing discovery, made partly in a woodshed. Never underestimate a shed.
